title: Bidirectional Dijkstra in San Francisco: Fast Routing ⚡
description: Watch Bidirectional Dijkstra sweep two frontiers—one from the start and one from the goal—until they meet. This visualization shows why route planning engines can scale shortest-path queries without exploring the whole map.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional Dijkstra: How Modern Route Planners Scale ⚡ (Why do we search from both ends?)

In this SoMa grid, the algorithm runs two Dijkstra searches at once:
1) Forward search expands from the start node with distances g_f.
2) Backward search expands from the goal node with distances g_b.
3) When the frontiers meet, we stitch paths via the best “meeting node” and stop early.

Deep technical idea: classic Dijkstra explores globally; bidirectional Dijkstra narrows the search radius by balancing work from both directions, often reducing expansions dramatically on realistic road graphs.

Takeaway: fewer popped nodes + earlier termination ≠ a different shortest path—just a smarter way to find it.

Debate: Should modern route planners always default to Bidirectional Dijkstra, or do A*/contraction hierarchies win in real-world deployments?
